title.title: The Correspondence of Esther Roberts Hunt Collins

msIdentifier.institution: Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College

projectDesc.p: The correspondence of Quaker minister Esther Roberts Hunt Collins is stored at the Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College. With the generous support of H. David and Joyce E. Hunt, Library staff scanned and transcribed these letters in 2024 and encoded the text in TEI.

div.p: I received thy kind letter sent by Joseph Townsend, which was indeed truly acceptable. I desire thee may not omit writing when there is opportunity. For my part there has often been misses, sometimes on one account & sometimes on another & sometimes the mind not prepared, for indeed there is many trials fallen to my lot, of different kinds. Oh, may I be preserved and rightly directed through them all, is the earnest desire of my mind. Thy letter was a cordial to a drooping mind, & the more so to find there was a prospect of a succession amongst the beloved youth in standing for the cause of the blessed truth. The account thee gave of the yearly meeting was comfortable, in particular that of your being brought to partake of the wine of the kingdom. Oh, what a favor! May we indeed, that are so far separated from you, labor more earnestly, to be found worthy to be fellow partakers thereof. For oh, may I not say that there has been of the wormwood & the gall fallen to some of our portions. I believe I should have wrote before, if I could have had a more agreeable account to have given, for it seems as if we were in a great measure, like unto the ground we read of, that was often watered, but still brought forth briars & thorns, & was right unto cursing, for it has been the case that the Lord’s servants have been sent unto us in an extraordinary manner. Laboring, rising up early & lying down late, undergoing great difficulty and hardship. But alas, how like the heath in the desert or the deaf adder are we, that the charmer's voice makes no impression.

Dear Brother, I wish not to anyway discourage discorage thee or any other that may feel anything towards us, for it is needful to be sensible we ail something, before we are willing to apply for a physician or to receive medicine when offered us.

It’s too much for to particularize matters amongst us, without it might be a means of helping them. Let me only say the head is much disordered, & it reaches to the feet, or lowest member. Some choice ones removed by death & their places not yet filled. Large numbers from different parts gathering to this land under our name, settling far & near, that I think never was there a greater need of lights or salt, good examples, sand- bearers than in this land at this day. It has been some time since writing the above having then a prospect of James French going in a short time, which has been put off by reason of the openness of the winter & he having the mo is not yet fit for the journey. Anna Vennable was married the 4th of 2nd month 1796 to Brian Taylor’s son, Brian, who came from Jersey about six years ago. As to thy name sake he was here I think with that worthy David Brook & another friend, I did not understand that John {he} had much to say in public. I had not much opportunity where he was.

8th 3rd month. Not finishing my letter & being disappointed in the opportunity of sending, I may further inform that Anna Vennable is married to one Brian Taylor they came from Jersey Thomas French has been keeping school at the meeting house by Jonas’s. James French has bought a saw mill & 30 acres of land joining us, & Crossly, Jacob with their families are living in my cabins & are busy at this time in making sugar. They expect to make 300 hundred weight. The old people are often complaining with complaints relative to old age.

John Crossly thinks he would not have missed coming for a great deal, & is in very good heart. His oldest daughter lives with me which is all the maid I have at present, that I seem to be very much tied to the cares of my own family, & at times feel too much cumber therewith. I feel a need of daily bread & of a renewal of strength and that wisdom which is profitable to direct us in all things. But oh, alas, after how many hindering cumbering things are in my way, may I be had in thy remembrance in times of favor, for I feel at times almost overwhelmed & fear that I shall not be able to stand and fulfill the many trusts that I am entrusted with. My children are growing fast up, & I feel so weak that I fear they will not have that precious part improved as it ought by seasonable advice and due care.

closer.salute: Oh, may may the veil be rent from our eyes and everything done away that hinders our journey heavenward, as the desire of thy poor Sister,

postscript.p: Although I have wrote a good deal, it seems as if it was but a small part of what at times might be done if I could but make it intelligible. I much desire thee to write when opportunity offers. Please to remember my love to friends & relations as though they were named, & accept a large share thyself. Cousin Rachel Cattle I expect is in Jersey, & her parents are as well as common I believe, & expect they will write to her.
